newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccan opposition says elections marred.
newsitem.headline: Moroccan opposition says elections marred.

text.p: Opposition parties whose candidates overall trailed in Morocco's local elections last week charged on Sunday that the poll had been marked by irregularities despite pledges by the authorities for a fair and transparent ballot.

"In many regions of Morocco, flagrant irregularities have been noted, perpetrated by agents of the authority...," the opposition Progress and Socialism Party (PSP) said through its mouthpiece Al Bayane.
It said the elections had not "held their promise" despite progress, and much remained to be done before the parliamentary ballot due in September.

The PSP is one of the four-party opposition Koutla group. On Sunday, with around 400 results still awaited out of more than 24,000 seats, the Koutla bloc had nearly 32 percent of the seats, compared to just over 20 percent in the last local poll in 1992.
Another Koutla member, the old guard Istiqlal party, had taken the largest number of seats, a total of 4,072.

But candidates for the pro-government rightist Wifaq group and centre-right group, led by the Independent National Rally (RNI), dominated with their respective tallies of 30.28 percent and 26.44 percent of the seats.
The RNI emerged as the second largest individual party, with 3,430 seats of those declared.
Independents and other small groups took around 11 percent.
Interior Minister Driss Basri told reporters on Saturday the elections had gone well, with a turnout of 74.88 percent of the more than 13 million electorate.

The Istiqlal party paper l'Opinion said on Sunday there had been cases of vote-buying, aggression, intervention by some officials and "passivity of the authorities in the face of certain irregularities." These had been reported to electoral bodies.

The semi-official Le Matin du Sahara newspaper said the elections had been carried out "in total transparency" with national and foreign observers declaring them "marked by the effective neutrality of the administration".
The local elections for 1,547 councils are the first of a series due to culminate in September with a general election for a new lower house of parliament.

Under the constitution, a new Upper House is to be formed with power to topple the government through a no-confidence motion, with 60 percent of its members being chosen by the local councils emerging from Friday's ballot.
Under planned decentralisation, regional councils will have more money and power to push development projects to end the disparity between town and country.
About half of the population of 28 million live in the countryside and have higher illiteracy rates, poorer health and lower living standards than people in the cities.

Basri told reporters: "The importance of these local elections ...lies in the fact that the commune now plays an essential role in the democratic edifice of the country and is called more than ever to contibute...to the development of the kingdom."
